items.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'Abundant'.
items.explanation: Abundant means existing in large quantities, so Plentiful is the closest synonym. Scarce, Meagre, Rare and Limited all suggest small quantities, the opposite sense.

items.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'Candid'.
items.explanation: Candid means truthful and straightforward, so Frank is the nearest meaning. Deceptive, Secretive, Evasive and Guarded all suggest holding back the truth.

items.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'Frugal'.
items.explanation: Frugal means careful with money and avoiding waste, so Thrifty is the closest synonym. Wasteful, Lavish, Extravagant and Spendthrift all describe the opposite habit.

items.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'Obstinate'.
items.explanation: Obstinate means refusing to change one's mind, so Stubborn is the nearest meaning. Flexible, Yielding, Compliant and Open-minded all describe willingness to change.

items.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'Transient'.
items.explanation: Transient means lasting only for a short time, so Temporary is the closest synonym. Permanent, Lasting, Eternal and Enduring all suggest long duration, the opposite sense.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to 'Transparent'.
items.explanation: Transparent means allowing light to pass through, so Opaque is its direct opposite. Clear, Lucid, See-through and Plain are all close in sense to transparent.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to 'Generous'.
items.explanation: Generous means willing to give freely, so Stingy is its opposite. Kind, Charitable, Liberal and Giving all share the generous sense.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to 'Ancient'.
items.explanation: Ancient means belonging to a very distant past, so Modern is its opposite. Old, Antique, Primitive and Age-old all point to the distant past.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to 'Brave'.
items.explanation: Brave means ready to face danger without fear, so Cowardly is its opposite. Bold, Fearless, Daring and Valiant are all synonyms of brave.

items.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to 'Humble'.
items.explanation: Humble means having a modest view of one's own importance, so Arrogant is its opposite. Modest, Meek, Unassuming and Simple all share the humble sense.

items.question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'to spill the beans'.
items.explanation: To spill the beans means to reveal a secret, usually by accident. The other options take the words literally and miss the figurative sense.

items.question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'once in a blue moon'.
items.explanation: Once in a blue moon means something that happens very rarely. The other options take the moon image literally and miss the figurative meaning.

items.question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'to break the ice'.
options: To ease social awkwardness at a first meeting
items.explanation: To break the ice means to ease the initial awkwardness when people meet for the first time. The other options take the ice image literally.

items.question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'a piece of cake'.
items.explanation: A piece of cake means a task that is very easy to do. The other options take the cake image literally or describe the opposite idea.

items.question: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'to beat around the bush'.
options: To avoid coming to the point
items.explanation: To beat around the bush means to avoid saying what one means directly, talking around a subject instead. The other options take the words literally.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences into a coherent paragraph. A: The library opens at nine every morning. B: Ravi reached the library at half past nine. C: He borrowed three books on Indian history. D: He returned home and began reading the first one.
items.explanation: The paragraph opens with the library opening time, then Ravi arriving, then borrowing the books, and ends with him going home to read. That order is A, B, C, D.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences into a coherent paragraph. A: Within a year, the new bridge changed the town completely. B: For decades, villagers crossed the river by boat. C: Traders from the far bank began to visit daily. D: The government built the bridge after years of requests.
items.explanation: The paragraph opens with the old way of crossing, then the building of the bridge, then its effect on the town, and ends with traders visiting daily. That order is B, D, A, C.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences into a coherent paragraph. A: She practised the violin for two hours every day. B: At first, the notes sounded harsh and uneven. C: After a year, she played her first concert. D: Her teacher praised her steady progress.
items.explanation: The paragraph starts with daily practice, then the poor early sound, then the teacher's praise, and ends with the first concert. That order is A, B, D, C.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences into a coherent paragraph. A: The train halted at a small station in the hills. B: Passengers stepped out to buy hot tea. C: The engine was refilled with water. D: After twenty minutes, the train moved on.
items.explanation: The train first halts, then the engine is refilled, then passengers buy tea, and finally the train moves on. That order is A, C, B, D.

items.question: Rearrange the following sentences into a coherent paragraph. A: The committee announced the results at noon. B: Students crowded around the notice board. C: Anita found her name at the top of the list. D: Her friends lifted her onto their shoulders in joy.
items.explanation: The paragraph opens with the announcement, then students crowding around, then Anita finding her name, and ends with her friends celebrating. That order is A, B, C, D.

items.question: Choose the word that best fits the blank. The judge listened ______ to both sides before giving his verdict.
items.explanation: Patiently fits because a judge must hear both sides with care before deciding. Carelessly, hurriedly, angrily and briefly all contradict the careful hearing the sentence describes.
items.topic: Verbal Ability - Fill in the Blanks

items.question: Choose the word that best fits the blank. The river ______ its banks after three days of continuous rain.
items.explanation: Overflowed fits because three days of continuous rain would make a river rise above its banks. Dried, narrowed, froze and emptied all describe the opposite effect.
items.topic: Verbal Ability - Fill in the Blanks

items.question: Choose the pair of words that best fits the blanks. The scientist's ______ research ______ the committee, which awarded her the grant.
items.explanation: Thorough and impressed fit together because careful, complete research would please a committee enough to award a grant. The other pairs describe poor research that would displease rather than impress.
items.topic: Verbal Ability - Fill in the Blanks

items.question: Choose the word that best fits the blank. The new manager was ______ for his honesty, and the staff trusted him completely.
items.explanation: Known fits because being known for honesty explains why the staff trusted him. Blamed, ignored, doubted and punished all suggest distrust, the opposite sense.
items.topic: Verbal Ability - Fill in the Blanks

items.question: Choose the pair of words that best fits the blanks. A teacher who ______ her students and ______ their questions patiently earns their respect.
items.explanation: Encourages and answers fit because a teacher who supports students and answers their questions patiently earns respect. The other pairs describe neglect or harshness, which would lose respect.
items.topic: Verbal Ability - Fill in the Blanks

items.question: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. (a) The number of students / (b) in the class / (c) are increasing / (d) every year.
items.explanation: The number is singular, so the verb must be is, not are. The error is in part (c). The other parts are grammatically correct.

items.question: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. (a) Neither the manager / (b) nor his assistants / (c) was present / (d) at the meeting.
items.explanation: With neither nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, assistants, which is plural, so the verb must be were, not was. The error is in part (c).

items.question: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. (a) She has been working / (b) here since / (c) five years / (d) and likes the job.
items.explanation: Since is used with a point in time, while a period of five years needs for. The error is in part (c); the correct form is for five years.

items.question: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. (a) The price of vegetables / (b) have risen / (c) sharply / (d) this month.
items.explanation: The subject is price, which is singular, so the verb must be has, not have. The error is in part (b).

items.question: Find the part of the sentence that has an error. (a) If I was you, / (b) I would accept / (c) the offer / (d) without delay.
items.explanation: In an unreal conditional, the verb must be were, not was, after if I. The error is in part (a); the correct form is If I were you.

items.question: Choose the best replacement for the underlined part. The teacher, as well as the students, were present in the hall.
items.explanation: The subject is the teacher, which is singular; as well as the students does not make it plural. The verb must be was present, so that replacement is correct.

items.question: Choose the best replacement for the underlined part. He did not know that his friend has left the city yesterday.
items.explanation: The leaving happened before the past moment of not knowing, and yesterday marks past time, so the past perfect had left is required. The other options keep the tense error.

items.question: Choose the best replacement for the underlined part. The committee members was divided on the issue.
items.explanation: Members is plural, so the verb must be were, not was. The correct replacement is were divided.

items.question: Choose the best replacement for the underlined part. She is one of the girls who has won the prize.
items.explanation: The relative clause refers to girls, a plural noun, so the verb must be have, not has. The correct replacement is have won.

items.question: Choose the best replacement for the underlined part. He is working here since 2019.
items.explanation: An action that began in 2019 and continues to the present needs the present perfect continuous, so has been working is the correct replacement.

items.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
items.explanation: Furniture is an uncountable noun with no plural form, and it takes a singular verb. The sentence with furniture is new is the only correct one.

items.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Divide the sweets among the two children.
Divide the sweets between the two children.
Divide the sweets between the two childrens.
Divide the sweets among the two child.
Divide the sweets between two child.
items.explanation: Between is used when two people or things are involved, and children is the correct plural form. The sentence with between the two children is the only correct one.

items.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
items.explanation: Many is used with countable plural nouns like students, and the verb must be plural. The sentence with many students were absent is the only correct one.

items.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: Either the clerk or the officers is responsible.
Either the clerk or the officers are responsible.
Either the clerk or the officers am responsible.
Either the clerk or the officer are responsible.
Either the clerks or the officer is responsible.
items.explanation: With either or, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, officers, which is plural, so are is correct. The sentence with either the clerk or the officers are responsible is the only correct one.

items.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: He gave me a valuable advice.
He gave me many valuable advices.
He gave me an valuable advice.
items.explanation: Advice is an uncountable noun, so it takes no article a and has no plural form. The sentence with he gave me valuable advice is the only correct one.

items.question: Choose the one word for: 'One who loves books'.
items.explanation: Bibliophile is a person who loves books. Bibliographer lists books, Bookkeeper keeps accounts, Librarian looks after a library, and Novelist writes novels.

items.question: Choose the one word for: 'Fear of closed spaces'.
items.explanation: Claustrophobia is the fear of closed spaces. Acrophobia is fear of heights, Agoraphobia is fear of open or crowded places, Hydrophobia is fear of water, and Xenophobia is fear of strangers.

items.question: Choose the one word for: 'One who can speak two languages'.
items.explanation: Bilingual is a person who can speak two languages. Monolingual speaks one language only, Polyglot speaks several, Linguist studies language, and Interpreter converts speech between languages.

items.question: Choose the one word for: 'A government by the rich'.
items.explanation: Plutocracy is rule by the wealthy. Democracy is rule by the people, Aristocracy is rule by nobles, Monarchy is rule by a king or queen, and Oligarchy is rule by a small group.

items.question: Choose the one word for: 'One who believes in fate'.
items.explanation: Fatalist is a person who believes that events are fixed by fate. Optimist expects good outcomes, Pessimist expects bad ones, Idealist follows ideals, and Realist accepts things as they are.

items.question: Hammer is to Nail as Screwdriver is to:
items.explanation: A hammer drives a nail, just as a screwdriver drives a screw. Wood and Wall are materials, Hammer is the first tool itself, and Drill is a different tool.

items.question: Cat is to Kitten as Dog is to:
items.explanation: A kitten is the young of a cat, just as a puppy is the young of a dog. Cub is the young of a lion, Calf of a cow, Lamb of a sheep, and Chick of a bird.

items.question: Winter is to Cold as Summer is to:
items.explanation: Winter is associated with cold, just as summer is associated with heat. Rain and Wind occur in any season, while Snow and Ice belong to winter.

items.question: Eye is to See as Ear is to:
items.explanation: The eye is the organ used to see, just as the ear is the organ used to hear. Smell, Touch and Taste belong to other senses, and Speak belongs to the mouth.

items.question: Seed is to Plant as Egg is to:
items.explanation: A seed grows into a plant, just as an egg hatches into a bird. Nest is where a bird lives, and Feather, Wing and Beak are parts of a bird.

items.set_title: Passage 1: Space Exploration and the Indian Space Programme
items.passage: On 23 August 2023, millions of Indians watched a small lander named Vikram touch down gently near the south pole of the Moon, and India became the fourth country in history to land softly on the Moon and the first to do so near its south pole. The landing was the crowning moment of Chandrayaan-3, but it was also the product of more than sixty years of patient work by the Indian Space Research Organisation, known as ISRO, which began with the launch of a tiny sounding rocket from a fishing village in Kerala in 1963. That rocket carried little more than scientific instruments, yet it marked the start of a programme built on a simple idea first put forward by Vikram Sarabhai, the father of the Indian space programme, that space technology must serve the daily needs of ordinary people. Sarabhai argued that India, a poor country with vast distances and frequent droughts and floods, needed satellites for communication, weather forecasting and the mapping of crops and water far more than it needed prestige in space. ISRO was formally set up in 1969, and its early years were spent learning the basics, building small satellites and learning how to launch them from the Sriharikota island on the Andhra Pradesh coast, now the Satish Dhawan Space Centre. The first Indian satellite, Aryabhata, was launched in 1975 with help from the Soviet Union, and within a few years India was building and launching its own satellites for television, telephone links and remote sensing. The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV, first flew in 1993 and became the workhorse of the programme, placing satellites into polar orbits with a reliability that won it commercial launch orders from many countries. Its larger brother, the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, or GSLV, gave India the ability to place heavy communication satellites into orbit above the equator without depending on foreign rockets. The programme took a bold turn in 2008, when Chandrayaan-1, India's first mission to the Moon, carried instruments that found evidence of water molecules on the lunar surface, a discovery that changed how scientists around the world thought about the Moon. Five years later, the Mars Orbiter Mission, popularly called Mangalyaan, reached Mars on its very first attempt in 2014, making India the first country to succeed on its first try and doing so at a cost far lower than similar missions by other space agencies. That low cost became a hallmark of ISRO, which builds its missions with small teams, simple designs and careful reuse of tested technology, proving that frugality and ambition can go together. Not every mission succeeded. Chandrayaan-2 in 2019 placed an orbiter around the Moon, but its lander crashed during the final descent, and ISRO spent four years studying the failure before trying again with Chandrayaan-3. The success of Chandrayaan-3 was followed within weeks by the launch of Aditya-L1, India's first mission to study the Sun, which now observes solar storms that can disturb satellites and power grids on Earth. Beyond exploration, satellites quietly serve India every day. Weather satellites warn fishermen of storms and farmers of rain, communication satellites bring television and internet to remote villages, and earth observation satellites map crops, forests, groundwater and the damage after floods and cyclones. The Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System, called NavIC, gives the country its own positioning service for transport, fishing boats and disaster relief, reducing dependence on foreign systems. The next steps are more ambitious. India is preparing Gaganyaan, its first human spaceflight, which will carry Indian astronauts into orbit, and it has announced plans for its own space station and a mission to Venus, while private Indian companies are now building rockets and satellites under a new policy that opens the sector to them. The programme also inspires a generation of students, who follow each launch live and dream of becoming engineers and scientists, and many of them will join a space industry that is now one of the fastest growing in the country. Critics sometimes ask whether a country with poverty should spend money on space, and the answer given by ISRO is that the money returns many times over in better weather forecasts, better communication, better disaster warning and new technology that finds its way into everyday life. The story of Indian space is therefore not only a story of rockets and the Moon, but a story of a country that used science to solve practical problems first, and only then reached for the stars.
items.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Chandrayaan-3 was the first Indian satellite
India should spend more money on space than on poverty removal
The PSLV is the only rocket India has ever built
Private companies should replace ISRO completely
The Indian space programme grew from practical needs into Moon, Mars and Sun missions
items.explanation: The passage traces the programme from its practical beginnings under Sarabhai through PSLV, Chandrayaan, Mangalyaan and Aditya-L1, which the first statement sums up. The other statements are too narrow or contradict the passage.

items.question: According to the passage, what made the Chandrayaan-3 landing special?
options: It carried astronauts to the Moon
It was the first satellite ever launched by India
India became the fourth country to land softly on the Moon and the first near its south pole
It was the cheapest mission in the world
items.explanation: The passage states that with Chandrayaan-3 India became the fourth country to land softly on the Moon and the first to do so near its south pole.

items.question: What did Chandrayaan-1 discover on the Moon?
options: A new element unknown on Earth
Gold deposits under the lunar surface
Signs of life in lunar craters
Evidence of water molecules on the lunar surface
items.explanation: The passage says Chandrayaan-1 carried instruments that found evidence of water molecules on the lunar surface, a discovery that changed how scientists thought about the Moon.

items.question: What was special about Mangalyaan, the Mars Orbiter Mission?
options: It was built by a private company
It carried Indian astronauts to Mars
It landed a rover on Mars
It reached Mars on its very first attempt, the first country to do so
items.explanation: The passage says Mangalyaan reached Mars on its very first attempt in 2014, making India the first country to succeed on its first try, and at a far lower cost than similar missions.

items.question: Why did low cost become a hallmark of ISRO, according to the passage?
options: Because ISRO spends nothing on testing its missions
Because ISRO buys all its rockets from other countries
Because ISRO builds missions with small teams, simple designs and reuse of tested technology
Because ISRO launches only very small satellites
Because the government refuses to fund space research
items.explanation: The passage says ISRO builds its missions with small teams, simple designs and careful reuse of tested technology, proving that frugality and ambition can go together.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a use of Indian satellites?
options: Exploring oil fields under the sea
Giving positioning services for transport and disaster relief
items.explanation: The passage mentions warning fishermen, mapping crops and groundwater, bringing television to villages, and the NavIC positioning service, but it never mentions exploring oil fields under the sea.

items.question: Which of the following best describes the tone of the passage?
items.explanation: The author admires the programme's achievements and explains them with facts and history, while also noting failures honestly, which is an admiring and informative tone.

items.question: What is the author most likely to agree with?
options: The Moon landing was a waste of money
India should stop all space missions until poverty ends
ISRO should only build rockets for other countries
Space spending is justified because it returns many times over in practical benefits
Private companies should be kept out of the space sector
items.explanation: The passage says ISRO's answer to critics is that the money returns many times over in better weather forecasts, communication, disaster warning and new technology.

items.passage: Long before the word industry was used, India clothed much of the world, and its fine cotton muslin was so delicate that a whole sari was said to pass through a ring. Traders from Rome, Arabia and China bought Indian cloth for centuries, and the weavers of Bengal, Gujarat and the Coromandel coast were famous for colours that did not fade and patterns that no other country could copy. That fame became a weakness under British rule, when machine-made cloth from Lancashire flooded Indian markets while Indian weavers paid heavy taxes, and the handloom industry that had fed millions of families shrank rapidly. The first cotton mills in India appeared in Bombay in the 1850s, and by the end of the century Bombay and Ahmedabad had become mill towns, with chimneys, shift whistles and rows of workers houses, but the mills served mainly the home market and left the village weaver behind. After independence in 1947, the government protected handlooms and small powerlooms, set up textile research institutes, and encouraged mills to modernise, yet the industry remained split between a modern mill sector and a vast decentralised sector of handlooms and powerlooms. Today that split still defines the industry. India is one of the largest producers of cotton in the world, grows jute in the east, silk in Karnataka and Kashmir, and wool in the north, and it is also a major producer of man-made fibres such as polyester and viscose. The textile and apparel industry employs more than four crore people, second only to agriculture, and it provides work to a large number of women, especially in spinning, weaving, garment stitching and embroidery. Exports of textiles and garments bring in billions of dollars each year, with the United States and Europe as the largest buyers, and Indian garments, home textiles and carpets are found in shops across the world. Some towns have become famous for a single product. Tiruppur in Tamil Nadu is known for knitwear, Surat in Gujarat for synthetic fabrics and dyeing, Panipat in Haryana for blankets and home furnishing, and Ludhiana in Punjab for woollen garments and hosiery. The handloom sector, though small in output, carries great cultural value, and saris from Kanchipuram, Banaras and Chanderi, shawls from Kashmir, and ikat from Odisha are prized for designs that have been passed down through generations of weaver families. Yet the industry faces serious problems. Many mills run old machines, power supply is unreliable in some states, and the cost of cotton and dyes rises and falls with world markets, making planning difficult for small units. Competition is fierce. Bangladesh and Vietnam, with lower wages and simpler labour rules, have taken large orders for basic garments, while China remains the largest exporter of textiles in the world. Indian exporters also struggle with slow port clearances, high logistics costs, and the need to meet strict environmental and labour standards set by foreign buyers, which small units find hard to follow. The government has responded with new schemes. The PM MITRA scheme is building large textile parks with modern infrastructure, the production linked incentive scheme rewards firms that invest in man-made fibre garments, and handloom weavers receive support for marketing, design and credit. Sustainability is becoming a new test. Buyers now ask for organic cotton, recycled polyester and dyes that do not pollute rivers, and some Indian firms have begun to use solar power, water recycling and natural dyes to meet these demands. Technology is changing the loom itself. Computer-aided design helps weavers create new patterns, automated looms raise output, and online platforms let small weavers sell directly to customers without middlemen. The future of the industry will depend on whether it can combine its old strengths, skilled hands, rich designs and abundant cotton, with modern machines, fast delivery and clean production. If it does, textiles can again become what they once were, one of India's greatest sources of employment, export earnings and pride, reaching from the village loom to the shops of the world.
items.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: India is the largest exporter of textiles in the world
Handloom weaving should be banned in favour of mills
The Indian textile industry has a long history and must combine old skills with modern methods to stay competitive
Cotton is the only fibre used in India
items.explanation: The passage covers the industry from ancient muslin through British decline, mills, present employment and exports, to its problems and future, which the first statement sums up.

items.question: According to the passage, which town is famous for knitwear?
items.explanation: The passage says Tiruppur in Tamil Nadu is known for knitwear, while Surat is known for synthetic fabrics, Panipat for blankets, and Ludhiana for woollen garments.

items.question: How many people does the textile and apparel industry employ, as per the passage?
options: More than four crore people, second only to agriculture
items.explanation: The passage states that the industry employs more than four crore people, second only to agriculture, and provides work to a large number of women.

items.question: Why did the handloom industry shrink under British rule?
options: The British banned all weaving in India
Indian weavers refused to weave cotton
Machine-made cloth from Lancashire flooded Indian markets while weavers paid heavy taxes
There was no cotton grown in India then
Indian cloth was too expensive for British buyers
items.explanation: The passage says machine-made cloth from Lancashire flooded Indian markets while Indian weavers paid heavy taxes, and the handloom industry that had fed millions shrank rapidly.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT true according to the passage?
options: Surat is known for synthetic fabrics and dyeing
Panipat is known for blankets and home furnishing
Ludhiana is known for silk saris
Kanchipuram is known for its saris
items.explanation: The passage says Ludhiana is known for woollen garments and hosiery, not silk saris. The other four statements are all given in the passage.

items.question: What does the passage suggest the industry must do to succeed in the future?
options: Stop exporting and sell only in India
Close all handloom units at once
Use only old machines and methods
Combine skilled hands, rich designs and cotton with modern machines, fast delivery and clean production
items.explanation: The passage says the future depends on combining old strengths, skilled hands, rich designs and abundant cotton, with modern machines, fast delivery and clean production.

items.question: What is the PM MITRA scheme doing, according to the passage?
options: Banning the import of foreign cloth
Building large textile parks with modern infrastructure
items.explanation: The passage says the PM MITRA scheme is building large textile parks with modern infrastructure, as part of the government response to the industry's problems.

items.question: The phrase 'that split still defines the industry' suggests that:
options: Handlooms and mills have merged into one sector
The industry has been divided into two countries
The divide between the modern mill sector and the decentralised handloom and powerloom sector persists today
The government has ended all support for handlooms
items.explanation: The split described earlier is between a modern mill sector and a vast decentralised sector of handlooms and powerlooms, and the passage says that divide still defines the industry today.

items.set_title: Passage 3: William Shakespeare and the Elizabethan Theatre
items.passage: When William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564, nobody in his small market town could have guessed that he would become the most famous writer in the English language. He was the son of a glove maker, attended the local grammar school, married Anne Hathaway at eighteen, and by his late twenties had arrived in London, where the theatre was the most popular entertainment of the age. London in the 1590s was a crowded, noisy city, and its theatres drew everyone from apprentices and sailors to merchants and courtiers, all paying a penny to stand in the open yard or more to sit in the covered galleries. Shakespeare joined the Lord Chamberlain's Men, a company of actors that later became the King's Men under James I, and he worked as actor, playwright and part owner of the Globe Theatre, which opened on the south bank of the Thames in 1599. The Globe was a round wooden building open to the sky, with a thrust stage that jutted into the yard, and its audience of up to three thousand people stood close to the actors, cheering, hissing and sometimes throwing things at the stage. There was almost no scenery, so the plays relied on words to create place and weather, and a single speech could turn the bare stage into a forest, a battlefield or a storm at sea. All the parts were played by men and boys, since women were not allowed on the public stage, and young boys played the heroines, wearing wigs and dresses and speaking lines of love and grief. Shakespeare wrote about thirty seven plays, and they fall into three broad groups, comedies that end in marriage, histories that retell the lives of English kings, and tragedies that end in death. His comedies, such as A Midsummer Night's Dream and Twelfth Night, are full of mistaken identity, clever servants and lovers who lose and find each other, and they end with music and marriage. His histories, such as Henry IV and Richard III, turn the past into drama, showing kings who win and lose crowns and the ordinary soldiers and citizens who pay for their ambition. His tragedies are his most famous works. Hamlet, a prince who cannot decide whether to avenge his father, Macbeth, a soldier destroyed by ambition, King Lear, an old king who divides his kingdom, and Othello, a general destroyed by jealousy, are still performed in every country in the world. What makes these plays last is not only their stories but their language. Shakespeare wrote in blank verse, unrhymed lines of ten syllables, and he invented or popularised hundreds of words and phrases that are still used today, from eyeball and bedroom to break the ice and wild goose chase. His characters speak as real people do, changing their minds, joking in the middle of sorrow, and asking questions that have no easy answer, and audiences recognise themselves in them across four centuries. The theatre of his time was a rough business. Actors rehearsed quickly, performed a different play each day, and shared the takings, while the authorities worried that theatres spread plague and disorder and closed them in times of sickness. Shakespeare also wrote long poems and 154 sonnets, short poems of fourteen lines that explore love, time and beauty, and many of them are still learned by schoolchildren. He retired to Stratford around 1613 and died there in 1616, at the age of fifty two, leaving a will that famously left his wife his second best bed, a detail that scholars still argue about. Seven years after his death, two of his fellow actors published the First Folio of 1623, a collection of thirty six of his plays, and without that book half his plays might have been lost for ever. Since then his work has been translated into every major language, performed in styles from Japanese kabuki to Bollywood film, and studied in schools across the world, yet the plays still work best as they were meant to be seen, spoken aloud by actors to a living audience. The Globe that stands in London today is a reconstruction, but when its audience stands in the yard as the audience did four hundred years ago, the distance between Shakespeare's time and ours seems very small.
items.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Shakespeare's life, his theatre and his language explain why his plays still live today
The Globe Theatre was the only theatre in London
Women were the best actors in Elizabethan theatre
items.explanation: The passage covers Shakespeare's life, the Globe, his three kinds of plays, his language and his lasting influence, which the first statement sums up.

items.question: In which year did the Globe Theatre open?
items.explanation: The passage says Shakespeare was part owner of the Globe Theatre, which opened on the south bank of the Thames in 1599.

items.question: How did Shakespeare's plays create place and weather, since there was almost no scenery?
options: Through words, with a single speech turning the bare stage into a forest or a storm
Through painted backdrops imported from Italy
Through large machines that changed the stage
Through films shown behind the actors
Through the audience imagining nothing at all
items.explanation: The passage says there was almost no scenery, so the plays relied on words to create place and weather, and a single speech could turn the bare stage into a forest, a battlefield or a storm at sea.

items.question: Who played the heroines in Shakespeare's plays?
options: Young boys, since women were not allowed on the public stage
items.explanation: The passage says all the parts were played by men and boys, since women were not allowed on the public stage, and young boys played the heroines.

items.question: What is blank verse, as described in the passage?
options: Poems with no words at all
items.explanation: The passage says Shakespeare wrote in blank verse, unrhymed lines of ten syllables. Short poems of fourteen lines are his sonnets, not blank verse.

items.question: What was the First Folio of 1623?
options: A collection of thirty six of Shakespeare's plays published by two fellow actors
A book of Shakespeare's letters to his wife
The first theatre built in London
A history of the King's Men
A collection of Shakespeare's sonnets only
items.explanation: The passage says two of his fellow actors published the First Folio of 1623, a collection of thirty six of his plays, and without it half his plays might have been lost.

items.question: According to the passage, what makes Shakespeare's plays last?
options: Their stories and their language, with characters who speak like real people
The fact that they were written in Latin
Their short length and simple plots
The support of the royal court alone
items.explanation: The passage says what makes the plays last is not only their stories but their language, and his characters speak as real people do, changing their minds and asking questions with no easy answer.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT true according to the passage?
options: Shakespeare wrote about thirty seven plays
Shakespeare was part owner of the Globe Theatre
Women played the heroines on the Elizabethan stage
The First Folio was published in 1623
items.explanation: The passage says women were not allowed on the public stage and young boys played the heroines, so that statement is false. The other four statements are all given in the passage.

items.question: What did Shakespeare leave his wife in his will, as per the passage?
items.explanation: The passage says he left a will that famously left his wife his second best bed, a detail that scholars still argue about.

items.set_title: Passage 4: Marie Curie and the Discovery of Radium
items.passage: Marie Curie was born Maria Sklodowska in Warsaw in 1867, when Poland was ruled by Russia and Polish girls were not allowed to study at university. She studied in secret, worked as a governess to pay for her sister's medical studies in Paris, and in 1891 she finally travelled to Paris herself, where she enrolled at the Sorbonne and lived in a cold attic room, studying through the night. At the Sorbonne she met Pierre Curie, a physicist, and they married in 1895, beginning a partnership in science that would change the world. For her doctoral research, Marie chose to study the strange rays that came from uranium, a heavy metal that fogged photographic plates even in the dark. She found that the rays came from the atom itself, not from any chemical reaction, and she gave the phenomenon a new name, radioactivity. Working with Pierre, she tested pitchblende, a dark ore that contained uranium, and found that it was far more radioactive than pure uranium, which meant that it must contain another, unknown element. In 1898 the Curies announced two new elements, polonium, named after Marie's homeland Poland, and radium, named from the Latin word for ray. To prove that radium existed, they had to isolate it, and that meant years of hard labour in a leaking shed, stirring tons of pitchblende in great iron pots and carrying heavy buckets of ore, with no protection from the rays. In 1902 they finally produced a tenth of a gram of pure radium chloride, a tiny amount that glowed faintly in the dark and proved beyond doubt that the new element was real. In 1903 Marie and Pierre Curie shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Henri Becquerel, and Marie became the first woman ever to win a Nobel Prize. Tragedy struck in 1906, when Pierre was killed in a street accident in Paris, and Marie, grief stricken, took over his teaching post at the Sorbonne, becoming the first woman to teach there. In 1911 she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry, for her work on radium and polonium, making her the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, a record that still stands. During the First World War, Marie used her knowledge to save lives. She fitted cars with X ray equipment, drove them herself to the front lines, and trained young women to take X ray pictures of wounded soldiers, so that doctors could find bullets and broken bones. She also founded the Radium Institute in Paris, where doctors studied how radiation could treat cancer, a use of radium that she had foreseen from the start. The work that made her famous also killed her. She had handled radioactive materials for years with bare hands, carrying samples in her pockets and keeping them in her desk, and in 1934 she died of aplastic anaemia, a disease of the blood caused by radiation. Her notebooks are still so radioactive today that they are kept in lead lined boxes, and anyone who wishes to read them must wear protective clothing. Her daughter Irene followed her into science and won a Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1935 with her husband, making the Curie family the most decorated scientific family in history. Marie Curie's life shows what persistence can do. A poor girl from an occupied country, barred from university, became through hard work and courage one of the greatest scientists who ever lived, and her work opened the way to nuclear physics, cancer treatment and the modern understanding of the atom.
items.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Marie Curie's persistence led her from a barred education in Poland to two Nobel Prizes and the discovery of radium
Marie Curie was the first woman to study at the Sorbonne
Radium was discovered by Pierre Curie alone
Marie Curie worked only on X ray machines
The Curies became rich from selling radium
items.explanation: The passage follows Marie Curie from her barred education in Warsaw through the discovery of polonium and radium, two Nobel Prizes, wartime X ray work and her death from radiation, which the first statement sums up.

items.question: What name did Marie Curie give to the rays from uranium?
items.explanation: The passage says she found that the rays came from the atom itself, and she gave the phenomenon a new name, radioactivity.

items.question: Which element did the Curies name after Marie's homeland, Poland?
items.explanation: The passage says the Curies announced polonium, named after Marie's homeland Poland, and radium, named from the Latin word for ray.

items.question: How many Nobel Prizes did Marie Curie win, and in which subjects?
options: Two, in Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911
Three, in Physics, Chemistry and Medicine
items.explanation: The passage says she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and won a second Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911, making her the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

items.question: What did Marie Curie do during the First World War?
options: She fitted cars with X ray equipment and drove them to the front lines
She discovered a new element at the front
She moved back to Warsaw permanently
She taught at the Sorbonne only
items.explanation: The passage says she fitted cars with X ray equipment, drove them herself to the front lines, and trained young women to take X ray pictures of wounded soldiers.

items.question: What is 18% of 450?
items.explanation: 18 percent of 450 is 0.18 times 450, which equals 81, so the required value is 81.

items.question: A man buys an article for Rs. 600 and sells it for Rs. 690. What is his profit percentage?
items.explanation: The profit is 690 minus 600, which is Rs. 90. As a percentage of the cost price 600, that is 90 divided by 600 times 100, which is 15 percent.

items.question: The ratio of two numbers is 4:7 and their sum is 99. What is the smaller number?
items.explanation: The two numbers are 4 parts and 7 parts of 99, so one part is 99 divided by 11, which is 9. The smaller number is 4 parts, which is 36.

items.question: A can do a job in 15 days and B can do it in 10 days. Working together, in how many days will they finish the job?
items.explanation: A does one fifteenth of the job per day and B does one tenth, so together they do one sixth per day. The whole job therefore takes 6 days.

items.question: A train 180 metres long crosses a pole in 12 seconds. What is its speed in km/h?
items.explanation: The train covers 180 metres in 12 seconds, which is 15 metres per second. Multiplying by 18 fifths to convert to km/h gives 54 km/h.
items.topic: Quantitative Aptitude - Time Speed and Distance

items.question: What is the simple interest on Rs. 6000 at 9% per annum for 4 years?
items.explanation: Simple interest is principal times rate times time divided by 100, which is 6000 times 9 times 4 divided by 100, giving Rs. 2160.

items.question: What is the compound interest on Rs. 8000 at 10% per annum compounded annually for 2 years?
items.explanation: The amount after two years is 8000 times 1.1 squared, which is Rs. 9680. The interest is 9680 minus 8000, which is Rs. 1680.

items.question: A number is increased by 30% and then decreased by 20%. What is the net percentage change?
items.explanation: A 30 percent rise followed by a 20 percent fall multiplies the value by 1.3 times 0.8, which is 1.04, so the net change is an increase of 4 percent.

items.question: A shopkeeper sells an article at a loss of 20%. If he had sold it for Rs. 240 more, he would have gained 10%. What is the cost price of the article?
items.explanation: Let the cost price be x. The two selling prices are 0.8x and 1.1x, and their difference is 240, so 0.3x equals 240 and x equals 800.

items.question: In what ratio must water be mixed with milk costing Rs. 60 per litre so that the mixture costs Rs. 45 per litre?
items.explanation: By alligation, the ratio of milk to water is 45 minus 0 to 60 minus 45, which is 45 to 15, or 3 to 1. So water to milk is 1 to 3.

items.question: If 5x - 7 = 3x + 11, what is the value of x?
items.explanation: Subtracting 3x from both sides gives 2x minus 7 equals 11, so 2x equals 18 and x equals 9.

items.question: What is the product of the roots of the equation x^2 - 7x + 12 = 0?
items.explanation: The equation factors as x minus 3 times x minus 4 equals zero, so the roots are 3 and 4, and their product is 12. This also follows from the rule that the product of the roots is the constant term.

items.question: What is the sum of the first 12 terms of the arithmetic progression 3, 7, 11, ...?
items.explanation: The first term is 3 and the common difference is 4. The sum of 12 terms is 6 times twice 3 plus 11 times 4, which is 6 times 50, giving 300.

items.question: The sum of an infinite geometric progression is 20 and its first term is 15. What is the common ratio?
items.explanation: The sum of an infinite GP is the first term divided by one minus the ratio, so 20 equals 15 divided by one minus r. That gives one minus r equal to three quarters, so r equals one quarter.

items.question: What is the area of a triangle with base 14 cm and height 10 cm?
items.explanation: The area of a triangle is half the base times the height, which is half of 14 times 10, giving 70 square cm.

items.question: What is the area of a circle of radius 14 cm? (Take pi = 22/7)
items.explanation: The area is pi times radius squared, which is 22 sevenths times 196, giving 616 square cm.

items.question: What is the perimeter of a rectangle of length 15 cm and breadth 9 cm?
items.explanation: The perimeter is twice the length plus breadth, which is twice 24, giving 48 cm.

items.question: What is the volume of a cuboid of length 6 cm, breadth 4 cm and height 5 cm?
items.explanation: The volume of a cuboid is length times breadth times height, which is 6 times 4 times 5, giving 120 cubic cm.

items.question: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 3:4:5. What is the largest angle?
items.explanation: The angles sum to 180 degrees, so one part is 180 divided by 12, which is 15 degrees. The largest angle is 5 parts, which is 75 degrees.

items.question: What is the HCF of 54 and 90?
items.explanation: 54 is 2 times 3 cubed and 90 is 2 times 3 squared times 5, so their highest common factor is 2 times 9, which is 18.

items.question: Which of the following numbers is divisible by 11?
items.explanation: A number is divisible by 11 if the difference of the sums of alternate digits is 0 or a multiple of 11. For 15246, the alternate sums are 9 and 9, so the difference is 0, while the others give differences of 3, 4, 5 and 6.

items.question: What is the remainder when 9^2 is divided by 7?
items.explanation: 9 squared is 81, and 81 divided by 7 gives 11 with a remainder of 4.

items.question: How many factors does 120 have?
items.explanation: 120 equals 2 cubed times 3 times 5, so the number of factors is 3 plus 1 times 1 plus 1 times 1 plus 1, which is 4 times 2 times 2, giving 16.

items.question: A die is thrown once. What is the probability of getting a number greater than 4?
items.explanation: The outcomes greater than 4 are 5 and 6, which are 2 of the 6 equally likely outcomes, so the probability is 2 sixths, which is one third.

items.question: Three coins are tossed together. What is the probability of getting exactly two heads?
items.explanation: Exactly two heads occurs in 3 of the 8 equally likely outcomes, HHT, HTH and THH, so the probability is 3 eighths.

items.question: In how many ways can 5 books be arranged in a row on a shelf?
items.explanation: The number of arrangements of 5 distinct books is 5 factorial, which is 5 times 4 times 3 times 2 times 1, giving 120.

items.question: In a school of 200 students, 120 play hockey, 90 play cricket, and 40 play both. How many play neither game?
items.explanation: The number who play at least one game is 120 plus 90 minus 40, which is 170. So the number who play neither is 200 minus 170, which is 30.

items.question: What is the value of (sqrt(7) + sqrt(2)) x (sqrt(7) - sqrt(2))?
items.explanation: This is the difference of squares: the square of root 7 minus the square of root 2, which is 7 minus 2, giving 5.

items.question: What is the value of cos 60 degrees?
items.explanation: The cosine of 60 degrees is a standard value, one half, which is 0.5.

items.question: A tower casts a shadow of 20 metres when the angle of elevation of the sun is 45 degrees. What is the height of the tower?
items.explanation: The height equals the shadow length times tan 45 degrees, which is 20 times 1, giving 20 metres.

items.question: Is x greater than 10? Statement I: x + 5 = 18. Statement II: x is less than 20.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives x equals 13, which is greater than 10. Statement II alone only says x is less than 20, which does not tell whether x is above or below 10. So statement I alone is sufficient.

items.question: Is P the mother of Q? Statement I: P is the wife of R. Statement II: R is the father of Q.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives only P's relation to R, and statement II alone gives only R's relation to Q. Together they show that P, as the wife of Q's father, is the mother of Q. So both statements together are sufficient.

items.question: What is the volume of a cuboid? Statement I: Its length is 6 cm and its breadth is 5 cm. Statement II: Its height is 4 cm.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Volume needs length, breadth and height. Statement I gives two of them and statement II gives the third, so together they give 6 times 5 times 4, which is 120 cubic cm. Both statements together are sufficient.

items.question: What is the present age of the father? Statement I: The father is 24 years older than his son. Statement II: The son is 18 years old.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives only the age difference, and statement II alone gives only the son's age. Together they give the father's age as 18 plus 24, which is 42. So both statements together are sufficient.

items.question: What is the correct time now? Statement I: The clock shows 5:30 but it is 25 minutes fast. Statement II: The clock was set right at 9:00 this morning.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone tells us the clock is 25 minutes fast, so the correct time is 5:05. Statement II alone gives no information about the current reading. So statement I alone is sufficient.

items.question: On which day of the week was 10 February 2025? Statement I: 1 February 2025 was a Saturday. Statement II: 2025 is not a leap year.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: 10 February is exactly 9 days after 1 February, which is one whole week plus two days, so it falls two days after Saturday, on Monday. Statement I alone is sufficient, and the leap year fact is irrelevant.

items.question: How many students play only cricket? Statement I: 80 students play cricket and 50 play football. Statement II: 30 students play both games and there are 120 students in all.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives the cricket total but not the overlap, and statement II alone gives the overlap but not the cricket total. Together, the number playing only cricket is 80 minus 30, which is 50. Both statements together are sufficient.

items.question: What is the area of a triangle? Statement I: Its base is 12 cm. Statement II: Its height is 8 cm.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: The area needs both the base and the height. Statement I gives only the base and statement II gives only the height, so together they give half of 12 times 8, which is 48 square cm.

items.question: Is y divisible by 12? Statement I: y is divisible by 3. Statement II: y is divisible by 4.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Divisibility by 3 alone does not guarantee divisibility by 12, and divisibility by 4 alone does not either. Together they do, since 3 and 4 are coprime and their product is 12. So both statements together are sufficient.

items.question: Is n an odd number? Statement I: n cubed is an odd number. Statement II: n plus 2 is an even number.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: If n cubed is odd then n must be odd, since the cube of an even number is even. If n plus 2 is even then n must be even, so the answer is no. Each statement alone settles the question, so either statement alone is sufficient.

items.question: What is the speed of the car? Statement I: It covers 180 km in 3 hours. Statement II: It covers 60 km in 1 hour.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives the speed as 180 divided by 3, which is 60 km/h. Statement II alone gives the speed as 60 divided by 1, which is also 60 km/h. Either statement alone is sufficient.

items.question: What is the cost price of an article? Statement I: Its selling price is Rs. 550 and the profit is 10%. Statement II: The profit on the article is Rs. 50.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives the cost price as 550 divided by 1.1, which is Rs. 500. Statement II alone gives only the profit, with no selling price, so it cannot give the cost price. So statement I alone is sufficient.

items.question: What is the average of five numbers? Statement I: The sum of the five numbers is 250. Statement II: Each of the five numbers is 50.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives the average as 250 divided by 5, which is 50. Statement II alone gives every number as 50, so the average is also 50. Either statement alone is sufficient.

items.question: What is the value of y? Statement I: 3y minus 4 equals 14. Statement II: y is an even number.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives 3y equals 18, so y equals 6. Statement II alone only says y is even, which does not fix its value. So statement I alone is sufficient.

items.question: What is the radius of a circle? Statement I: Its diameter is 14 cm. Statement II: Its circumference is 44 cm.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives the radius as half the diameter, which is 7 cm. Statement II alone gives the radius from 2 pi r equals 44, which is also 7 cm. Either statement alone is sufficient.

items.question: How many electric vehicles did the five brands sell together in 2025?

diagram.caption: Electric vehicles sold by five brands in 2025 (in thousands)

items.explanation: The five brands sold 48, 36, 54, 28 and 42 thousand vehicles, and their sum is 208 thousand.

items.question: Which brand sold the most electric vehicles in 2025?
items.explanation: The bar for Eco Motors reaches 54 thousand vehicles, which is higher than every other brand shown in the chart.

items.question: VoltAuto sold how many percent more vehicles than Terra Motors?
items.explanation: VoltAuto sold 48 thousand and Terra Motors sold 42 thousand, a difference of 6 thousand. As a percentage of 42, that is 6 divided by 42 times 100, which is about 14.3 percent.

items.question: What was the average number of electric vehicles sold per brand?
items.explanation: The five brands sold 208 thousand vehicles together, and 208 divided by 5 is 41.6 thousand per brand.

items.question: GreenDrive's sales were what percentage of the total sales of all five brands?
items.explanation: GreenDrive sold 36 thousand of the 208 thousand vehicles sold in all, and 36 divided by 208 times 100 is about 17.3 percent.

items.question: What was the total rainfall in the four cities together in July?

diagram.caption: Rainfall in four cities, June to August (in mm)

items.explanation: In July the rainfall was 620 mm in Mumbai, 90 mm in Chennai, 340 mm in Kolkata and 180 mm in Delhi, and their sum is 1230 mm.

items.question: Which city received the highest total rainfall over the three months?
items.explanation: Mumbai received 550 plus 620 plus 480, which is 1650 mm, more than Kolkata with 930 mm, Delhi with 430 mm and Chennai with 360 mm.

items.question: By what percentage did rainfall in Delhi increase from June to July?
items.explanation: Rainfall in Delhi rose from 90 mm in June to 180 mm in July, an increase of 90 mm. As a percentage of 90, that is 90 divided by 90 times 100, which is 100 percent.

items.question: What was the total rainfall in Chennai over the three months?
items.explanation: Chennai received 120 mm in June, 90 mm in July and 150 mm in August, and their sum is 360 mm.

items.question: Mumbai's rainfall in August was what percentage of its total rainfall over the three months?
items.explanation: Mumbai received 480 mm in August out of a three-month total of 1650 mm, and 480 divided by 1650 times 100 is about 29.1 percent.

items.set_title: Set 3: Tourists Visiting a National Park
items.question: In which year was the number of tourists the lowest?

diagram.caption: Tourists visiting a national park (in lakh), 2019 to 2023

items.explanation: The line dips to 9 lakh tourists in 2020, which is lower than the number in every other year shown.

items.question: How many tourists visited the national park in all over the five years?
items.explanation: The yearly numbers were 12, 9, 15, 18 and 21 lakh tourists, and their sum is 75 lakh.

items.question: By what percentage did the number of tourists increase from 2020 to 2021?
items.explanation: Tourists rose from 9 lakh in 2020 to 15 lakh in 2021, an increase of 6 lakh. As a percentage of 9, that is 6 divided by 9 times 100, which is about 66.7 percent.

items.question: By what percentage did the number of tourists increase from 2022 to 2023?
items.explanation: Tourists rose from 18 lakh in 2022 to 21 lakh in 2023, an increase of 3 lakh. As a percentage of 18, that is 3 divided by 18 times 100, which is about 16.7 percent.

items.question: If the number of tourists grows in 2024 by the same percentage as it grew from 2022 to 2023, how many lakh tourists will visit in 2024?
items.explanation: The growth from 2022 to 2023 was 3 lakh on 18 lakh, which is one sixth. Applying the same growth to 21 lakh gives 21 times 7 sixths, which is 24.5 lakh.
